toc.title: How the chart is laid out
Using it to find your state
Don't save it for a crisis

blocks.p: SSIEC stands for state, sensation, impulse, emotion, and cognition. It's a guide I created on how to understand those five things and how they all connect. My hope is that it gives you some clarity on what's going on in your inner world.

I designed it mainly for therapists and coaches to use in their sessions, to help themselves and their clients build a new language, a shared language. You can also use it for yourself. I've started to use it, and it's been pretty darn helpful so far.

What's a Stucknaut? It's us. It's those of us who are looking into ourselves, into our internal world, and figuring out, "Hey, what's going on in there, and how can I meet my goals? But also, how can I feel what I feel? How can I recognize what I think and how I feel without judgment? How can I just be with myself?"

To do that, you need the right tools, and I think SSIEC is a very central one. State, sensation, impulse, emotion, and cognition are domains that come up in therapy very often, and I'd assume they come up quite often in your own meditative Stucknaut work too. I know they come up a lot for me as I look inward as best I can.

blocks.h: How the chart is laid out

blocks.p: SSIEC is a chart. Across the top are five columns: state, sensation, impulse, emotion, and cognition. Down the side are six rows for the polyvagal states: safe and social, flight and fight, shutdown, freeze, play, and stillness. Each state has its own colored band running across its row, and that band connects the polyvagal state to the words in the other columns.
Flight and fight are both sympathetic, so I put them in the same band. We could separate them, but for clarity and simplicity I kept them together.

The idea is to get more of an understanding of how these domains interact, and specifically to connect them to your primary states and mixed states. I've found that really useful for telling these things apart.
Take safe and social. Reading across that row:

ul: Sensation: warm, shimmering, light, open, aware, and a few more.
Impulse: co-regulate, connect, socialize. Those are maybe synonyms, but they're ways to describe what you have an impulse to do from your safe and social state.
Emotion: connected, confident, loving, playful, joy, and a couple of others.

blocks.p: The cognition column doesn't tell you what your thoughts actually are. I can't tell you that. It's the flavor of your thoughts. From safe and social, your thoughts will probably be more optimistic, and there's also a good chance there's a very logical component. That doesn't mean you're not empathetic. It's not all or nothing. But I think you'll be able to use logic from your safe and social state, and more effectively.

That's true for all the other rows as well: these are the flavor of your cognitions, not your cognitions in and of themselves. For flight and fight, the cognition flavor is thinking about the past and the future, labeling, dismissing, and judging, to name a few. For shutdown, it's slow, clouded, hopeless.

All of the columns, the S and the I and the E and the C, stem from your polyvagal state. The state is the primary driving factor. Even before that comes neuroception, I suppose. But for the sake of this, it all comes from the state.

So in play, the sensations are energized, ease, fluid. Those sensations come from the mixed state of play. If you feel those things, that's an indicator that you have access to play. In shutdown, the cognitions are slow, clouded, hopeless. The flavor of those cognitions isn't there for no reason. It's there because it's connected to an autonomic state of shutdown.

I'd also put them in a flow, though that's not extremely important to me. From the state, you have a sensation, and then you have an impulse. If you don't act on that impulse, then you have an emotion, and that emotion flavors your cognitions more. I'd say emotion and cognition are both definitely flavored by a frustrated impulse, one that's not being acted on. And I think emotion and cognition are very circular. They feed into each other.
So state to sensation to impulse makes a lot of sense. Is it super important that you understand it as flowing in that direction? I don't think so. Like I said, I do think the state is primary.

blocks.h: Using it to find your state

blocks.p: What really matters is that you can notice what's happening within you. Here's how to use the chart:

ol: Find one word that fits what you're going through, in any column.
Track across that band to the state column, to see which state it belongs to.
Look along the rest of that row for other words: sensations, impulses, emotions you might not have been able to name.

blocks.p: Let's say you're talking to your therapist, or your client is talking to you, and maybe you both use polyvagal language. They say, "I don't know what state I'm in, but I feel a lot of rage. I've been feeling like I just want to snap and hurt someone."

You can both find rage in the emotion column, in the freeze band, and track it across to freeze. "Okay, sounds like you're in a freeze mixed state." That means there's an element of shutdown, or immobility, but also an element of high mobility, sympathetic flight and fight energy. For rage, I'd say it's more of a flavor of fight. Then you can use the rest of the freeze row to identify other sensations or emotions, and maybe an impulse.
Here's a different example. A client says, "I don't know what's happening within me. I just feel a lot of numbness. I just feel kind of blah."

Numb is in the emotion column, and it connects to the state of shutdown, which makes a lot of sense. Now you can help your client find other words they may be struggling to identify. From that numb shutdown state, there may be an impulse to disconnect, to immobilize and just be still for a moment, or to reduce stimulation. That last one isn't on the chart, but reducing stimulation could be an impulse as well. There may be a sensation of floating, or of emptiness or hollowness.

So you can use SSIEC to identify what's happening within you, and also to build the language around it and broaden your understanding of what's happening within you in that moment. If I can identify this one thing, maybe I can look across the row and identify other things that can help me feel what I'm going through right now.

SSIEC is pretty comprehensive, but it's not final. You could totally add words to it. I actually had to remove a lot of words to make space for other concepts, and there are way more that could fit, especially in the emotion column, which is jam-packed. Use it as a starting guide: here are some common words that fit these domains. In no way do I want you to be limited by them.

At first glance, it might seem a bit overwhelming. Just saying, "Hey, look at this and pick something," might be too much. But as you practice using it, and get familiar with the states and the columns, it becomes easier. It can become pretty quick to use.

blocks.h: Don't save it for a crisis

blocks.p: Don't wait to use this in a crisis. When someone's overwhelmed, that's not what we want to do. Use it when things aren't overwhelming, when there's more capacity to be reflective: to sit and think and look at these things, to feel what's happening within, to identify and share new words, and to work together on that level.
So practice there. Don't bring it out when someone's in the throes of a panic attack. That probably wouldn't be super helpful.
